entries.c8b97c70fea82ea33a0133f10c54f4634f82f1de: <div sID="gen16878" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="58" osisID="Isa.58" sID="Isa.58"/> <div eID="gen16878" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16879" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen16880" type="x-p"/> The prophet, in this chapter, has his commission and charge renewed to reprove the sinners in Zion, particularly the hypocrites, to show them their transgressions, <reference osisRef="Isa.58.1">ver. 1</reference>. It is intended for admonition and warning to all hypocrites, and is not to be confined to those of any one age. Some refer it primarily to those at that time when Isaiah prophesied; see <reference osisRef="Isa.33.14">chap. xxxiii. 14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.29.13">xxix. 13</reference>. Others to the captives in Babylon, the wicked among them, to whom the prophet had declared there was no peace <reference osisRef="Isa.57.21">ch. lvii. 21</reference>. Against the terror of that word they thought to shelter themselves with their external performances, particularly their fastings, which they kept up in Babylon, and for some time after their return to their own land, <reference osisRef="Zech.7.3">Zech. vii. 3</reference>, &c. The prophet therefore here shows them that their devotions would not entitle them to peace while their conversations were not at all of a piece with them. Others think it is principally intended against the hypocrisy of the Jews, especially the Pharisees before and in our Saviour's time: they boasted of their fastings, but Christ (as the prophet here) showed them their transgressions (<reference osisRef="Matt.23.1-Matt.23.39">Matt. xxiii.</reference>), much the same with those they are here charged with. Observe, I. The plausible profession of religion which they made, <reference osisRef="Isa.58.2">ver. 2</reference>. II. The boasts they made of that profession, and the blame they laid upon God for taking no more notice of it, <reference osisRef="Isa.58.3">ver. 3</reference>. III. The sins they are charged with, which spoiled the acceptableness of their fasts, <reference osisRef="Isa.58.4-Isa.58.5">ver. 4, 5</reference>. IV. Instructions given them how to keep fasts aright, <reference osisRef="Isa.58.6-Isa.58.7">ver. 6, 7</reference>. V. Precious promises made to those who do so keep fasts, <reference osisRef="Isa.58.8-Isa.58.12">ver. 8-12</reference>. VI. The like precious promises made to those that sanctify sabbaths aright, <reference osisRef="Isa.58.13-Isa.58.14">ver. 13, 14</reference>.
entries.ee19437e0ef5634093aa93ae0db83d9cb90c6ae8: <div eID="gen16880" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen16879" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">A Charge against the People. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 706.)</title> <div sID="gen16881" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Cry aloud, spare not, lift up thy voice like a trumpet, and show my people their transgression, and the house of Jacob their sins. <hi type="super">2</hi> Yet they seek me daily, and delight to know my ways, as a nation that did righteousness, and forsook not the ordinance of their God: they ask of me the ordinances of justice; they take delight in approaching to God. <div eID="gen16881" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16882" type="x-p"/> When our Lord Jesus promised to send the Comforter he added, <hi type="italic">When he shall come he shall convince</hi> (<reference osisRef="John.16.7-John.16.8">John xvi. 7, 8</reference>); for conviction must prepare for comfort, and must also separate between the precious and the vile, and mark out those to whom comfort does not belong. God had appointed this prophet to comfort his people (<reference osisRef="Isa.40.1">ch. xl. 1</reference>); here he appoints him to convince them, and show them their sins. <div eID="gen16882" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16883" type="x-p"/> I. He must tell them how very bad they really were, <reference osisRef="Isa.58.1">v. 1</reference>. 1. He must deal faithfully and plainly with them. "Though they are called <hi type="italic">the people of God</hi> and <hi type="italic">the house of Jacob,</hi> though they wear an honourable title and character, by which they are interested in many glorious privileges, yet do not flatter them, but show them their transgressions and their sins, be particular in telling them their faults, what sins are committed among them, which they do not know of, nay, what sins are committed by them which they do not acknowledge to be sins; though in some things they are reformed, let them know that in other things they are still as bad as ever. Show them their transgressions and their sins, that is, all their transgressions in their sins, their sins and all the aggravations of them," <reference osisRef="Lev.16.21">Lev. xvi. 21</reference>. Note, (1.) God sees sin in his people, in the house of Jacob, and is displeased with it. (2.) They are often unapt and unwilling to see their own sins, and need to have them shown them, and to be told, <hi type="italic">Thus and thus thou hast done.</hi> 2. He must be vehement and in good earnest herein, must <hi type="italic">cry aloud, and not spare,</hi> not spare them (not touch them with his reproofs as if he were afraid of hurting them, but search the wound to the bottom, lay it bare to the bone), not spare himself or his own pains, but cry as loud as he can; though he spend his strength and waste his spirits, though he get their ill-will by it and get himself into an ill name, yet he must not spare. He must lift up his voice like a trumpet, to make those hear of their faults that were apt to be deaf when admonition was addressed to them. He must give his reproofs in the most powerful and pressing manner possible, as one who desired to be heeded. The trumpet does not give an uncertain sound, but, though loud and shrill, is intelligible; so must his alarms be, giving them warning of the fatal consequences of sin, <reference osisRef="Ezek.33.3">Ezek. xxxiii. 3</reference>. <div eID="gen16883" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16884" type="x-p"/> II. He must acknowledge how very good they seemed to be, notwithstanding (<reference osisRef="Isa.58.2">v. 2</reference>): <hi type="italic">Yet they seek me daily.</hi> When the prophet went about to show them their transgressions they pleaded that they could see no transgressions which they were guilty of; for they were diligent and constant in attending on God's worship—and what more would he have of them? Now, <div eID="gen16884" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16885" type="x-p"/> 1. He owns the matter of fact to be true. As far as hypocrites do that which is good, they shall not be denied the praise of it; let them make their best of it. It is owned that they have a form of godliness. (1.) They go to church, and observe their hours of prayer: <hi type="italic">They seek me daily;</hi> they are very constant in their devotions and never omit them nor suffer any thing to put them by. (2.) They love to hear good preaching; <hi type="italic">They delight to know my ways,</hi> as Herod, who heard John gladly, and the stony ground, that received the seed of the word with joy; it is to them <hi type="italic">as a lovely song,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ezek.33.32">Ezek. xxxiii. 32</reference>. (3.) They seem to take great pleasure in the exercises of religion and to be in their element when they are at their devotions: <hi type="italic">They delight in approaching to God,</hi> not for his sake to whom they approach, but for the sake of some pleasing circumstance, the company, or the festival. (4.) They are inquisitive concerning their duty and seem desirous only to know it, making no question but that then they should do it: <hi type="italic">They ask of me the ordinances of justice,</hi> the rules of piety in the worship of God, the rules of equity in their dealings with men, both which are ordinances of justice. (5.) They appear to the eye of the world as if they made conscience of doing their duty: <hi type="italic">They are as a nation that did righteousness and forsook not the ordinances of their God;</hi> others took them for such, and they themselves pretended to be such. Nothing lay open to view that was a contradiction to their profession, but they seemed to be such as they should be. Note, Men may go a great way towards heaven and yet come short; nay, may go to hell with a good reputation. But, <div eID="gen16885" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16886" type="x-p"/> 2. He intimates that this was so far from being a cover or excuse for their sin that really it was an aggravation of it: "Show them their sins which they go on in notwithstanding their knowledge of good and evil, sin and duty, and the convictions of their consciences concerning them."
entries.58ddfa903c70bb1cc44e8157c7e2be95a2375c6f: <div eID="gen16886" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">A Charge against the People. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 706.)</title> <div sID="gen16887" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">3</hi> Wherefore have we fasted, <hi type="italic">say they,</hi> and thou seest not? <hi type="italic">wherefore</hi> have we afflicted our soul, and thou takest no knowledge? Behold, in the day of your fast ye find pleasure, and exact all your labours. <hi type="super">4</hi> Behold, ye fast for strife and debate, and to smite with the fist of wickedness: ye shall not fast as <hi type="italic">ye do this</hi> day, to make your voice to be heard on high. <hi type="super">5</hi> Is it such a fast that I have chosen? a day for a man to afflict his soul? <hi type="italic">is it</hi> to bow down his head as a bulrush, and to spread sackcloth and ashes <hi type="italic">under him?</hi> wilt thou call this a fast, and an acceptable day to the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> ? <hi type="super">6</hi> <hi type="italic">Is</hi> not this the fast that I have chosen? to loose the bands of wickedness, to undo the heavy burdens, and to let the oppressed go free, and that ye break every yoke? <hi type="super">7</hi> <hi type="italic">Is it</hi> not to deal thy bread to the hungry, and that thou bring the poor that are cast out to thy house? when thou seest the naked, that thou cover him; and that thou hide not thyself from thine own flesh? <div eID="gen16887" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16888" type="x-p"/> Here we have, I. The displeasure which these hypocrites conceived against God for not accepting the services which they themselves had a mighty opinion of (<reference osisRef="Isa.58.3">v. 3</reference>): <hi type="italic">Wherefore have we fasted, say they, and thou seest not?</hi> Thus they went in the way of Cain, who was angry at God, and resented it as a gross affront that his offering was not accepted. Having gone about to put a cheat upon God by their external services, here they go about to pick a quarrel with God for not being pleased with their services, as if he had not done fairly or justly by them. Observe, 1. How they boast of themselves, and magnify their own performances: "<hi type="italic">We have fasted, and afflicted our souls;</hi> we have not only sought God daily (<reference osisRef="Isa.58.2">v. 2</reference>), but have kept some certain times of more solemn devotion." Some think this refers to the yearly fast (which was called <hi type="italic">the day of atonement</hi>), others to their arbitrary occasional fasts. Note, It is common for unhumbled hearts to be proud of their professions of humiliation, as the Pharisee (<reference osisRef="Luke.18.12">Luke xviii. 12</reference>), <hi type="italic">I fast twice in the week.</hi> 2. What they expected from their performances. They thought God should take great notice of them, and own himself a debtor to them for their services. Note, It is a common thing for hypocrites, while they perform the external services of religion, to promise themselves that acceptance with God which he has promised only to the sincere; as if they must be accepted of course, or for a compliment. 3. How heinously they take it that God had not put some particular marks of his favour upon them, that he had not immediately delivered them out of their troubles and advanced them to honour and prosperity. They charge God with injustice and partiality, and seem resolved to throw up their religion, and justify themselves in doing so with this, that they had found no <hi type="italic">profit in praying</hi> to God, <reference osisRef="Job.21.14-Job.21.15">Job xxi. 14, 15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Mal.3.14">Mal. iii. 14</reference>. Note, Reigning hypocrisy often breaks out in daring impiety and an open contempt and reproach of God and religion for that which the hypocrisy itself must bear all the blame of. Sinners reflect upon religion as a hard and melancholy service, and on which there is nothing to be got by, when really it is owing to themselves that it seems so to them, because they are not sincere in it. <div eID="gen16888" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16889" type="x-p"/> II. The true reason assigned why God did not accept their fastings, nor answer the prayers they made on their fast-days; it was because they did not fast aright—<hi type="italic">to God, even to him,</hi> <reference osisRef="Zech.7.5">Zech. vii. 5</reference>. They fasted indeed, but they persisted in their sins, and did not, as the Ninevites, turn every one from his evil way; but <hi type="italic">in the day of their fast,</hi> notwithstanding the professed humiliations and covenants of that day, they went on to <hi type="italic">find pleasure,</hi> that is, to do whatsoever seemed right in their own eyes, lawful or unlawful, <hi type="italic">quicquid libet, licet—making their inclinations their law;</hi> though they seemed to afflict their souls, they still gratified their lusts as much as ever. 1. They were as covetous and unmerciful as ever: "<hi type="italic">You exact all your labours</hi> from your servants, and will neither release them according to the law nor relax the rigour of their servitude." This was their fault before the captivity, <reference osisRef="Jer.34.8-Jer.34.9">Jer. xxxiv. 8, 9</reference>. It was no less their fault after their captivity, notwithstanding all their solemn fasts, <reference osisRef="Neh.5.5">Neh. v. 5</reference>. "<hi type="italic">You exact all your dues,</hi> your <hi type="italic">debts</hi>" (so some read it); "you are as rigorous and severe in extorting what you demand from those that are poor as ever you were, though it was at the close of the yearly fast that the release was proclaimed." 2. They were contentious and spiteful (<reference osisRef="Isa.58.4">v. 4</reference>): <hi type="italic">Behold, you fast for strife and debate.</hi> When they proclaimed a fast to deprecate God's judgments, they pretended to search for those sins which provoked God to threaten them with his judgments, and under that pretence perhaps particular persons were falsely accused, as Naboth in the day of Jezebel's fast, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.21.12">1 Kings xxi. 12</reference>. Or the contending parties among them upon those occasions were bitter and severe in their reflections one upon another, one side crying out, "It is owing to you," and the other, "It is owing to you, that our deliverance is not wrought." Thus, instead of judging themselves, which is the proper work of a fast-day, they condemned one another. They <hi type="italic">fasted for strife,</hi> with emulation which should make the most plausible appearance on a fast-day and humour the matter best. Nor was it only tongue-quarrels that were fomented in the times of their fasting, but they came to blows too: <hi type="italic">You smite with the fist of wickedness.</hi> The cruel task-masters beat their servants, and the creditors their insolvent debtors, whom they delivered to the tormentors; they abused poor innocents <hi type="italic">with wicked hands.</hi> Now while they thus <hi type="italic">continued in sin,</hi> in those very sins which were directly contrary to the intention of a fasting day, (1.) God would not allow them the use of such solemnities: "<hi type="italic">You shall not fast</hi> at all if you fast <hi type="italic">as you do this day, causing your voice to be heard on high,</hi> in the heat of your clamours one against another, or in your devotions, which you perform so as to make them to be taken notice of for ostentation. <hi type="italic">Bring me no more</hi> of these empty, noisy, <hi type="italic">vain oblations,</hi>" <reference osisRef="Isa.1.13">ch. i. 13</reference>. Note, Those are justly forbidden the honour of a profession of religion that will not submit to the power of it. (2.) He would not accept of them in the use of them: "<hi type="italic">You shall not fast,</hi> that is, it shall not be looked upon as a fast, nor shall the voice of your prayers on those days be heard on high in heaven." Note, Those that fast and pray, and yet go on in their wicked ways, do but mock God and deceive themselves. <div eID="gen16889" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16890" type="x-p"/> III. Plain instructions given concerning the true nature of a religious fast. <div eID="gen16890" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16891" type="x-p"/> 1. In general, a fast is intended, (1.) For the honouring and pleasing of God. It must be such a performance as he has chosen (<reference osisRef="Isa.58.5">v. 5</reference>); it must be <hi type="italic">an acceptable day to the Lord,</hi> in the duties of which we must study to approve ourselves to him and obtain his favour, else it is not a fast, else there is nothing done to any purpose. (2.) For the humbling and abasing of ourselves. A fast is <hi type="italic">a day to afflict the soul;</hi> if it do not express a genuine sorrow for sin, and do not promote a real mortification of sin, it is not a fast; the law of the day of atonement was that on that day they should <hi type="italic">afflict their souls,</hi> <reference osisRef="Lev.16.29">Lev. xvi. 29</reference>. That must be done on a fast-day which is a real affliction to the soul, as far as it is yet unregenerate and unsanctified, though a real pleasure and advantage to the soul as far as it is itself. <div eID="gen16891" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16892" type="x-p"/> 2. It concerns us therefore to enquire, on a fast-day, what it is that will be acceptable to God, and afflictive to our corrupt nature, and tending to its mortification. <div eID="gen16892" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16893" type="x-p"/> (1.) We are here told negatively what is not the fast that God has chosen, and which does not amount to the afflicting of the soul. [1.] It is not enough to look demure, to put on a grave and melancholy aspect, to bow down the head like a bulrush that is withered and broken: as the hypocrites, that were <hi type="italic">of a sad countenance, and disfigured their faces, that they might appear unto men to fast,</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.6.16">Matt. vi. 16</reference>. Hanging down the head did indeed well enough become the publican, whose heart was truly humbled and broken for sin, and who therefore, in token of that, <hi type="italic">would not so much as lift up his eyes to heaven</hi> (<reference osisRef="Luke.18.13">Luke xviii. 13</reference>); but when it was only mimicked, as here, it was justly ridiculed: it is but <hi type="italic">hanging down the head like a bulrush,</hi> which nobody regards or takes any notice of. As the hypocrite's humiliations are but like the hanging down of a bulrush, so his elevations in his hopes are but like the <hi type="italic">flourishing of a bulrush</hi> (<reference osisRef="Job.8.11-Job.8.12">Job viii. 11, 12</reference>), which, <hi type="italic">while it is yet in its greenness, withers before any other herb.</hi> [2.] It is not enough to do penance, to mortify the body a little, while the body of sin is untouched. It is not enough for a man <hi type="italic">to spread sackcloth and ashes under him,</hi> which may indeed give him some uneasiness for the present, but will soon be forgotten when he returns to <hi type="italic">stretch himself upon his beds of ivory,</hi> <reference osisRef="Amos.6.4">Amos vi. 4</reference>. <hi type="italic">Wilt thou call this a fast?</hi> No, it is but the shadow and carcase of a fast. <hi type="italic">Wilt thou call this an acceptable day to the Lord?</hi> No, it is so far from being so that the hypocrisy of it is an abomination to him. Note, The shows of religion, though they show ever so fair in the eye of the world, will not be accepted of God without the substance of it. <div eID="gen16893" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16894" type="x-p"/> (2.) We are here told positively what is the fast that God has chosen, what that is which will recommend a fast-day to the divine acceptance, and what is indeed afflicting the soul, that is, crushing and subduing the corrupt nature. It <hi type="italic">is not afflicting the soul for a day</hi> (as some read it, <reference osisRef="Isa.58.5">v. 5</reference>) that will serve; no, it must be the business of our whole lives. It is here required, [1.] That we be just to those with whom we have dealt hardly. The fast that God has chosen consists in reforming our lives and undoing what we have done amiss (<reference osisRef="Isa.58.6">v. 6</reference>): <hi type="italic">To loose the bands of wickedness,</hi> the bands which we have wickedly tied, and by which others are bound out from their right or bound down under severe usage. Those which perhaps were at first bands of justice, tying men to pay a due debt, become, when the debt is exacted with rigour from those whom Providence has reduced and emptied, <hi type="italic">bands of wickedness,</hi> and they must be loosed, or they will bring us into bonds of guilt much more terrible. It is <hi type="italic">to undo the heavy burden</hi> laid on the back of the poor servant, under which he is ready to sink. It is <hi type="italic">to let the oppressed go free</hi> from the oppression which makes his life bitter to him. "Let the prisoner for debt that has nothing to pay be discharged, let the vexatious action be quashed, let the servant that is forcibly detained beyond the time of his servitude be released, and thus <hi type="italic">break every yoke;</hi> not only let go those that are wrongfully kept under the yoke, but break the yoke of slavery itself, that it may not serve again another time nor any by made again to serve under it." [2.] That we be charitable to those that stand in need of charity, <reference osisRef="Isa.58.7">v. 7</reference>. The particulars in the <reference osisRef="Isa.58.6">former verse</reference> <hi type="italic">may</hi> be taken as acts of charity, that we not only release those whom we have unjustly oppressed—that is justice, but that we contribute to the rescue and ransom of those that are oppressed by others, to the release of captives and the payment of the debts of the poor; but those in this verse are <hi type="italic">plainly</hi> acts of charity. This then is the fast that God has chosen. <hi type="italic">First,</hi> To provide food for those that want it. This is put first, as the most necessary, and which the poor can but a little while live without. It is <hi type="italic">to break thy bread to the hungry.</hi> Observe, "It must be <hi type="italic">thy</hi> bread, that which is honestly got (not that which thou hast robbed others of), the bread which thou thyself hast occasion for, the bread of thy allowance." We must deny ourselves, that we may have to give to him that needeth. "Thy bread which thou hast spared from thyself and thy family, on the fast-day, if that, or the value of it, be not given to the poor, it is the miser's fast, which he makes a hand of; it is fasting for the world, not for God. This is the true fast, to break thy bread to the hungry, not only to give them that which is already broken meat, but to break bread on purpose for them, to give them loaves and not to put them off with scraps." <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> To provide lodging for those that want it: It is <hi type="italic">to take care of the poor that are cast out,</hi> that are forced from their dwelling, turned out of house and harbour, <hi type="italic">are cast out as rebels</hi> (so some critics render it), that are attainted, and whom therefore it is highly penal to protect. "If they suffer unjustly, make no difficulty of sheltering them; do not only find out quarters for them and pay for their lodging elsewhere, but, which is a greater act of kindness, bring them to thy own house, make them thy own guests. Be not forgetful to entertain strangers: for though thou mayest not, as some have done, thereby entertain angels, thou mayest entertain Christ himself, who will recompense it in the resurrection of the just. <hi type="italic">I was a stranger and you took me in." Thirdly,</hi> To provide clothing for those that want it: "<hi type="italic">When thou seest the naked, that thou cover him,</hi> both to shelter him from the injuries of the weather and to enable him to appear decently among his neighbours; give him clothes to come to church in, and in these and other instances <hi type="italic">hide not thyself from thy own flesh.</hi>" Some understand it more strictly of a man's own kindred and relations: "If those of thy own house and family fall into decay, thou art <hi type="italic">worse than an infidel</hi> if thou dost not <hi type="italic">provide</hi> for them." <reference osisRef="1Tim.5.8">1 Tim. v. 8</reference>. Others understand it more generally; all that partake of the human nature are to be looked upon as our own flesh, for have we not all one Father? And for this reason we must not hide ourselves from them, not contrive to be out of the way when a poor petitioner enquires for us, not look another way when a moving object of charity and compassion presents itself; let us remember that they are flesh of our flesh and therefore we ought to sympathize with them, and in doing good to them we really do good to our own flesh and spirit too in the issue; for thus <hi type="italic">we lay up for ourselves a good foundation,</hi> a good bond, <hi type="italic">for the time to come.</hi>
entries.b7d5d3dd02dd0542128761c6171e3ae742e98c94: <div eID="gen16894" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">A Charge against the People; Encouragement to Israelites Indeed. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 706.)</title> <div sID="gen16895" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">8</hi> Then shall thy light break forth as the morning, and thine health shall spring forth speedily: and thy righteousness shall go before thee; the glory of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> shall be thy rereward. <hi type="super">9</hi> Then shalt thou call, and the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> shall answer; thou shalt cry, and he shall say, Here I <hi type="italic">am.</hi> If thou take away from the midst of thee the yoke, the putting forth of the finger, and speaking vanity; <hi type="super">10</hi> And <hi type="italic">if</hi> thou draw out thy soul to the hungry, and satisfy the afflicted soul; then shall thy light rise in obscurity, and thy darkness <hi type="italic">be</hi> as the noonday: <hi type="super">11</hi> And the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> shall guide thee continually, and satisfy thy soul in drought, and make fat thy bones: and thou shalt be like a watered garden, and like a spring of water, whose waters fail not. <hi type="super">12</hi> And <hi type="italic">they that shall be</hi> of thee shall build the old waste places: thou shalt raise up the foundations of many generations; and thou shalt be called, The repairer of the breach, The restorer of paths to dwell in. <div eID="gen16895" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16896" type="x-p"/> Here are precious promises for those to feast freely and cheerfully upon by faith who keep the fast that God has chosen; let them know that God will make it up to them. Here is, <div eID="gen16896" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16897" type="x-p"/> I. A further account of the duty to be done in order to our interest in these promises (<reference osisRef="Isa.58.9-Isa.58.10">v. 9, 10</reference>); and here, as before, it is required that we both do justly and love mercy, that we cease to do evil and learn to do well. 1. We must abstain from all acts of violence and fraud. "Those must be <hi type="italic">taken away from the midst of thee,</hi> from the midst of <hi type="italic">thy person,</hi> out of <hi type="italic">thy heart</hi>" (so some); "thou must not only refrain from the practice of injury, but mortify in thee all inclination and disposition towards it." Or <hi type="italic">from the midst of thy people.</hi> Those in authority must not only not be oppressive themselves, but must do all they can to prevent and restrain oppression in all within their jurisdiction. They must not only <hi type="italic">break the yoke</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.58.6">v. 6</reference>), but take away the yoke, that those who have been oppressed may never be re-enslaved (as they were <reference osisRef="Jer.34.10-Jer.34.11">Jer. xxxiv. 10, 11</reference>); they must likewise <hi type="italic">forbear threatening</hi> (<reference osisRef="Eph.6.9">Eph. vi. 9</reference>) and take away the <hi type="italic">putting forth of the finger,</hi> which seems to have been then, as sometimes with us, a sign of displeasure and the indication of a purpose to correct. Let not the finger be put forth to point at those that are poor and in misery, and so to expose them to contempt; such expressions of contumely as are provoking, and the products of ill-nature, ought to be banished from all societies. And let them not <hi type="italic">speak vanity,</hi> flattery or fraud, to one another, but let all conversation be governed by sincerity. Perhaps that dissimulation which is the bane of friendship is meant by the putting forth of the finger (as <reference osisRef="Prov.6.13">Prov. vi. 13</reference> by <hi type="italic">teaching with the finger</hi>), or it is putting forth the finger with the ring on it, which was the badge of authority, and which therefore they produced when they spoke iniquity, that is, gave unrighteous sentences. 2. We must abound in all acts of charity and beneficence. We must not only give alms according as the necessities of the poor require, but, (1.) We must give freely and cheerfully, and from a principle of charity. We must <hi type="italic">draw out our soul to the hungry</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.58.10">v. 10</reference>), not only draw out the money and reach forth the hand, but do this from the heart, heartily, and without grudging, from a principle of compassion and with a tender affection to such as we see to be in misery. Let the heart go along with the gift; for God loves a cheerful giver, and so does a poor man too. When our Lord Jesus healed and fed the multitude it was as having compassion on them. (2.) We must give plentifully and largely, so as not to tantalize, but to <hi type="italic">satisfy, the afflicted soul:</hi> "Do not only feed the hungry, but gratify the desire of the afflicted, and, if it lies in your power, make them easy." What are we born for, and what have we our abilities of body, mind, and estate for, but to do all the good we can in this world with them? And the poor we have always with us. <div eID="gen16897" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16898" type="x-p"/> II. Here is a full account of the blessings and benefits which attend the performance of this duty. If a person, a family, a people, be thus disposed to every thing that is good, let them know for their comfort that they shall find God their bountiful rewarder and what they lay out in works of charity shall be abundantly made up to them. 1. God will surprise them with the return of mercy after great affliction, which shall be as welcome as the light of the morning after a long and dark night (<reference osisRef="Isa.58.8">v. 8</reference>): <hi type="italic">"Then shall thy light break forth as the morning</hi> and (<reference osisRef="Isa.58.10">v. 10</reference>) <hi type="italic">thy light shall rise in obscurity.</hi> Though thou hast been long buried alive thou shalt recover thy eminency; though long overwhelmed with grief, thou shalt again look pleasant as the dawning day." Those that are cheerful in doing good God will make cheerful in enjoying good; and this also is a special <hi type="italic">gift of God,</hi> <reference osisRef="Eccl.2.24">Eccl. ii. 24</reference>. Those that have shown mercy shall find mercy. Job, who in his prosperity had done a great deal of good, had friends raised up for him by the Lord when he was reduced, who helped him with their substance, so that his light rose in obscurity. "Not only thy light, which is sweet, but thy health too, or the healing of the wounds thou hast long complained of, shall spring forth speedily; all thy grievances shall be redressed, and thou shalt renew thy youth and recover thy vigour." Those that have helped others out of trouble will obtain help of God when it is their turn. 2. God will put honour upon them. Good works shall be recompensed with a good name; this is included in that <hi type="italic">light which rises out of obscurity.</hi> Though a man's extraction be mean, his family obscure, and he has no external advantages to gain him honour, yet, if he do good in his place, that will procure him respect and veneration, and his darkness shall by this means become <hi type="italic">as the noon-day,</hi> that is, he shall become very eminent and shine brightly in his generation. See here what is the surest way for a man to make himself illustrious; let him study to do good. He that would be the greatest of all, and best-loved, let him by humility and industry make himself a servant of all. "<hi type="italic">Thy righteousness shall answer for thee</hi> (as Jacob says, <reference osisRef="Gen.30.33">Gen. xxx. 33</reference>), that is, it shall silence reproaches, nay, it shall bespeak thee more praises than thy humility can be pleased with." He that has <hi type="italic">given to the poor, his righteousness</hi> (that is, the honour of it) <hi type="italic">endures for ever,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.112.9">Ps. cxii. 9</reference>. 3. They shall always be safe under the divine protection: "<hi type="italic">Thy righteousness shall go before</hi> thee as thy vanguard, to secure thee from enemies that charge thee in the front, and <hi type="italic">the glory of the Lord shall be thy rearward,</hi> the gathering host, to bring up those of thee that are weary and are left behind, and to secure thee from the enemies, that, like Amalek, fall upon thy rear." Observe, How good people are safe on all sides. Let them look which way they will, behind them or before them; let them look backward or forward; they see themselves safe, and find themselves easy and quiet from the fear of evil. And observe what it is that is their defence; it is their righteousness, and the glory of the Lord, that is, as some suppose, Christ; for it is by him that we are justified, and God is glorified. He it is that goes before us, and is the captain of our salvation, as he is the Lord our righteousness; he it is that is our rearward, on whom alone we can depend for safety when our sins pursue us and are ready to take hold on us. Or, "God himself in his providence and grace shall both go before thee as thy guide to conduct thee, and attend thee as thy rearward to protect thee, and this shall be the reward of thy righteousness and so shall be for the glory of the Lord as the rewarder of it." 4. God will be always nigh unto them, to hear their prayers, <reference osisRef="Isa.58.9">v. 9</reference>. As, on the one hand, he that shuts his ears to the cry of the poor shall himself cry and God will not hear him; so, on the other hand, he that is liberal to the poor, his prayers shall come up with his alms for a memorial before God, as Cornelius's did (<reference osisRef="Acts.10.4">Acts x. 4</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Then shalt thou call,</hi> on thy fast-days, which ought to be days of prayer, <hi type="italic">and the Lord shall answer,</hi> shall give thee the things thou callest to him for; <hi type="italic">thou shalt cry</hi> when thou art in any distress or sudden fright, <hi type="italic">and he shall say, Here I am.</hi>" This is a very condescending expression of God's readiness to hear prayer. When God calls to us by his word it becomes us to say, <hi type="italic">Here we are; what saith our Lord unto his servants?</hi> But that God should say to us, <hi type="italic">Behold me, here I am,</hi> is strange. When we cry to him, as if he were at a distance, he will let us know that he is near, even at our right hand, nearer than we thought he was. <hi type="italic">It is I, be not afraid.</hi> When danger is near our protector is nearer, <hi type="italic">a very present help.</hi> "Here I am, ready to give you what you want, and do for you what you desire; what have you to say to me?" God is attentive to the prayers of the upright, <reference osisRef="Ps.130.2">Ps. cxxx. 2</reference>. No sooner do they call to him than he answers, <hi type="italic">Ready, ready.</hi> Wherever they are praying, God says, "Here I am hearing; I am <hi type="italic">in the midst of you.</hi>" He is <hi type="italic">nigh unto them in all things,</hi> <reference osisRef="Deut.4.7">Deut. iv. 7</reference>. 6. God will direct them in all difficult and doubtful cases (<reference osisRef="Isa.58.11">v. 11</reference>): <hi type="italic">The Lord shall guide thee continually.</hi> While we are here, in the wilderness of this world, we have need of continual direction from heaven; for, if at any time we be left to ourselves, we shall certainly miss our way; and therefore it is to those who are good in God's sight that he gives the wisdom which in all cases is profitable to direct, and he will be to them <hi type="italic">instead of eyes,</hi> <reference osisRef="Eccl.2.26">Eccl. ii. 26</reference>. His providence will make their way plain to them, both what is their duty and what will be most for their comfort. 6. God will give them abundance of satisfaction in their own minds. As the world is a wilderness in respect of wanderings, so that they need to be guided continually, so also is it in respect of wants, which makes it necessary that they should have continual supplies, as Israel in the wilderness had not only the pillar of cloud to guide them continually, but manna and water out of the rock to satisfy their souls in drought, <hi type="italic">in a dry and thirsty land where no water is,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.63.1">Ps. lxiii. 1</reference>. To a good man God gives not only wisdom and knowledge, but joy; he is satisfied in himself with the testimony of his conscience and the assurances of God's favour. "These will <hi type="italic">satisfy thy soul,</hi> will put gladness into thy heart, even <hi type="italic">in the drought</hi> of affliction; <hi type="italic">these will make fat thy bones,</hi> and fill them with marrow, will give thee that pleasure which will be a support to thee as the bones to the body, that joy of the Lord which will be thy strength. <hi type="italic">He shall give thy bones rest</hi>" (so some read it), "rest from the pain and sickness which they have laboured under and been chastened with;" so it agrees with that promise made to the merciful. The Lord will <hi type="italic">make all his bed in his sickness,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.41.3">Ps. xli. 3</reference>. "<hi type="italic">Thou shalt be like a watered garden,</hi> so flourishing and fruitful in graces and comforts, <hi type="italic">and like a spring of water,</hi> like a garden that has a spring of water in it, <hi type="italic">whose waters fail not</hi> either in droughts or in frosts." The principle of holy love in those that are good shall be a <hi type="italic">well of living water,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.4.14">John iv. 14</reference>. As a spring of water, though it is continually sending forth its streams, is yet always full, so the charitable man abounds in good as he abounds in doing good and is never the poorer for his liberality. He that waters shall himself be watered. 7. They and their families shall be public blessings. It is a good reward to those that are fruitful and useful to be rendered more so, and especially to have those who descend from them to be so too. This is here promised (<reference osisRef="Isa.58.12">v. 12</reference>): "Those that now are of thee, thy princes, and nobles, and great men, shall have such authority and influence as they never had;" or, "<hi type="italic">Those that</hi> hereafter <hi type="italic">shall be of thee,</hi> thy posterity, shall be serviceable to their generation, as thou art to thine." It completes the satisfaction of a good man, as to this world, to think that those that come after him shall be doing good when he is gone. 1. They shall re-edify cities that have been long in ruins, <hi type="italic">shall build the old waste places,</hi> which had lain so long desolate that the rebuilding of them was quite despaired of. This was fulfilled when the captives, after their return, repaired the cities of Judah, and dwelt in them, and many of those in Israel too, which had lain waste ever since the carrying away of the ten tribes. 2. They shall carry on and finish that good work which was begun long before, and shall be helped over the obstructions which had retarded the progress of it: <hi type="italic">They shall raise up</hi> to the top that building <hi type="italic">the foundation of</hi> which was laid long since and has been for <hi type="italic">many generations</hi> in the rearing. This was fulfilled when the building of the temple was revived after it had stood still for many years, <reference osisRef="Ezra.5.2">Ezra v. 2</reference>. Or, "They shall raise up foundations which shall continue for many generations yet to come;" they shall do that good which shall be of lasting consequence. 3. They shall have the blessing and praise of all about them: "<hi type="italic">Thou shalt be called</hi> (and it shall be to thy honour) <hi type="italic">the repairer of the breach,</hi> the breach made by the enemy in the wall of a besieged city, which whoso has the courage and dexterity to make up, or make good, gains great applause." Happy are those who make up the breach at which virtue is running out and judgments are breaking in. "Thou shalt be <hi type="italic">the restorer of paths,</hi> safe and quiet paths, not only to travel in, but <hi type="italic">to dwell in,</hi> so safe and quiet that people shall make no difficulty of building their houses by the road-side." The sum is that, if they keep such fasts as God has chosen, he will settle them again in their former peace and prosperity, and there shall be none to make them afraid. See <reference osisRef="Zech.7.5 Zech.7.9 Zech.8.3-Zech.8.5">Zech. vii. 5, 9; viii. 3-5</reference>. It teaches us that those who do justly and love mercy shall have the comfort thereof in this world.
entries.fe8e77ccfae812fce8984e305310f2e2b1c7a3e7: <div eID="gen16898" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Sanctification of the Sabbath. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 706.)</title> <div sID="gen16899" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">13</hi> If thou turn away thy foot from the sabbath, <hi type="italic">from</hi> doing thy pleasure on my holy day; and call the sabbath a delight, the holy of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , honourable; and shalt honour him, not doing thine own ways, nor finding thine own pleasure, nor speaking <hi type="italic">thine own</hi> words: <hi type="super">14</hi> Then shalt thou delight thyself in the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> ; and I will cause thee to ride upon the high places of the earth, and feed thee with the heritage of Jacob thy father: for the mouth of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> hath spoken <hi type="italic">it.</hi> <div eID="gen16899" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16900" type="x-p"/> Great stress was always laid upon the due observance of the sabbath day, and it was particularly required from the Jews when they were captives in Babylon, because by keeping that day, in honour of the Creator, they distinguished themselves from the worshippers of the gods that have not made the heavens and the earth. See <reference osisRef="Isa.56.1-Isa.56.2">ch. lvi. 1, 2</reference>, where keeping the sabbath is joined, as here, with <hi type="italic">keeping judgment</hi> and <hi type="italic">doing justice.</hi> Some, indeed, understand this of the day of atonement, which they think is the fast spoken of in the former part of the chapter, and which is called a <hi type="italic">sabbath of rest,</hi> <reference osisRef="Lev.23.32">Lev. xxiii. 32</reference>. But, as the fasts before spoken of seem to be those that were occasional, so this sabbath is doubtless the weekly sabbath, that great sign between God and his professing people—his appointing it a sign of his favour to them and their observing it a sign of their obedience to him. Now observe here, <div eID="gen16900" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16901" type="x-p"/> I. How the sabbath is to be sanctified (<reference osisRef="Isa.58.13">v. 13</reference>); and, there remaining still a sabbatism for the people of God, this law of the sabbath is still binding to us on our Lord's day. <div eID="gen16901" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16902" type="x-p"/> 1. Nothing must be done that puts contempt upon the sabbath day, or looks like having mean thoughts of it, when God has so highly dignified it. We must <hi type="italic">turn away our foot from the sabbath,</hi> from trampling upon it, as profane atheistical people do, from travelling on that day (so some); we must turn away our foot <hi type="italic">from doing our pleasure on that holy day,</hi> that is, from living at large, and taking a liberty to do what we please on sabbath days, without the control and restraint of conscience, or from indulging ourselves in the pleasures of sense, in which the modern Jews wickedly place the sanctification of the sabbath, though it is as great a profanation of it as any thing. On sabbath days we must not walk in <hi type="italic">our own ways</hi> (that is, not follow our callings), not <hi type="italic">find our own pleasure</hi> (that is, not follow our sports and recreations); nay, we must not <hi type="italic">speak our own words,</hi> words that concern either our callings or our pleasures; we must not allow ourselves a liberty of speech on that day as on other days, for we must then mind God's ways, make religion the business of the day; we must choose the things that please him; and speak his words, speak of divine things as we sit in the house and walk by the way. In all we say and do we must put a difference between this day and other days. <div eID="gen16902" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16903" type="x-p"/> 2. Every thing must be done that puts an honour on the day and is expressive of our high thoughts of it. We must call it <hi type="italic">a delight,</hi> not a <hi type="italic">task and a burden;</hi> we must delight ourselves in it, in the restraints it lays upon us and the services it obliges us to. We must be in our element when we are worshipping God, and in communion with him. <hi type="italic">How amiable are thy tabernacles, O Lord of hosts!</hi> We must not only count it a delight, but call it so, must openly profess the complacency we take in the day and the duties of it. We must call it so to God, in thanksgiving for it and earnest desire of his grace to enable us to do the work of the day in its day, because we delight in it. We must call it so to others, to invite them to come and share in the pleasure of it; and we must call it so to ourselves, that we may not entertain the least thought of wishing the sabbath gone that we may sell corn. We must call it <hi type="italic">the Lord's holy day, and honourable.</hi> We must call it <hi type="italic">holy,</hi> separated from common use and devoted to God and to his service, must call it <hi type="italic">the holy of the Lord,</hi> the day which he has sanctified to himself. Even in Old-Testament times the sabbath was called <hi type="italic">the Lord's day,</hi> and therefore it is fitly called so still, and for a further reason, because it is the <hi type="italic">Lord Christ's day,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rev.1.10">Rev. i. 10</reference>. It is holy because it is the Lord's day, and upon both accounts it is honourable. It is a beauty of holiness that is upon it; it is ancient, and its antiquity is its honour; and we must make it appear that we look upon it as honourable by honouring God on that day. We put honour upon the day when we give honour to him that instituted it, and to whose honour it is dedicated. <div eID="gen16903" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16904" type="x-p"/> II. What the reward is of the sabbath—sanctification, <reference osisRef="Isa.58.14">v. 14</reference>. If we thus <hi type="italic">remember the sabbath day to keep it holy,</hi> <div eID="gen16904" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16905" type="x-p"/> 1. We shall have the comfort of it; the work will be its own wages. <hi type="italic">If we call the sabbath a delight, then shall we delight ourselves in the Lord;</hi> he will more and more manifest himself to us as the delightful subject of our thoughts and meditations and the delightful object of our best affections. Note, The more pleasure we take in serving God the more pleasure we shall find in it. If we go about duty with cheerfulness, we shall go from it with satisfaction and shall have reason to say, "It is good to be here, good to draw near to God." <div eID="gen16905" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16906" type="x-p"/> 2. We shall have the honour of it: <hi type="italic">I will cause thee to ride upon the high places of the earth,</hi> which denotes not only a great security (as that, <reference osisRef="Isa.32.16">ch. xxxii. 16</reference>, <hi type="italic">He shall dwell on high</hi>), but great dignity and advancement. "Thou shalt ride in state, shalt appear conspicuous, and the eyes of all thy neighbours shall be upon thee." It was said of Israel, when God led them triumphantly out of Egypt, that <hi type="italic">he made them to ride on the high places of the earth,</hi> <reference osisRef="Deut.32.12-Deut.32.13">Deut. xxxii. 12, 13</reference>. Those that honour God and his sabbath he will thus honour. If God by his grace enable us to live above the world, and so to manage it as not only not to be hindered by it, but to be furthered and carried on by it in our journey towards heaven, then he makes us <hi type="italic">to ride on the high places of the earth.</hi> <div eID="gen16906" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16907" type="x-p"/> 3. We shall have the profit of it: I will <hi type="italic">feed thee with the heritage of Jacob thy father,</hi> that is, with all the blessings of the covenant and all the precious products of Canaan (which was a type of heaven), for these were the heritage of Jacob. Observe, The heritage of believers is what they shall not only be portioned with hereafter, but fed with now, fed with the hopes of it, and not flattered, fed with the earnests and foretastes of it; and those that are so fed have reason to say that they are well fed. In order that we may depend upon it, it is added, "<hi type="italic">The mouth of the Lord has spoken it;</hi> you may take God's word for it, for he cannot lie nor deceive; what his mouth has spoken his hand will give, his hand will do, and not one iota or tittle of his good promise shall fall to the ground." <hi type="italic">Blessed, therefore,</hi> thrice blessed, <hi type="italic">is he that doeth this, and lays hold on it, that keeps the sabbath from polluting it.</hi>  <chapter eID="Isa.58"/> <div eID="gen16907" type="x-p"/>

entries.6cb57b405771d73ce52a1c5df5eb121ff1c8d8dc: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9413"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 58</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Isa.58.1-Isa.58.14">Is 58:1-14</reference>. Reproof of the Jews for Their Dependence on Mere Outward Forms of Worship.</title> <div sID="gen16309" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9413"/><hi type="bold">1. aloud--</hi>Hebrew, "with the throat," that is, with full voice, not merely from the lips (<reference osisRef="1Sam.1.13">1Sa 1:13</reference>). Speak loud enough to arrest attention.<div eID="gen16309" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16310" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">my people--</hi>the Jews in Isaiah's time, and again in the time of our Lord, more zealous for externals than for inward holiness. Rosenmuller thinks the reference to be to the Jews in the captivity practising their rites to gain God's favor and a release; and that hence, sacrifices are not mentioned, but only fasting and Sabbath observance, which they could keep though far away from the temple in Jerusalem. The same also applies to their present dispersion, in which they cannot offer sacrifices, but can only show their zeal in fastings, &c. Compare as to our Lord's time, <reference osisRef="Matt.6.16">Mt 6:16</reference>, <reference osisRef="Matt.6.23">23</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.18.12">Lu 18:12</reference>. <div eID="gen16310" type="x-p"/>
entries.57d831f3d5323c09adcb802a49c8840d0fc02a7e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9414"/><div sID="gen16311" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9414"/>2. Put the stop at "ways"; and connect "as a nation that," &c. with what follows; "As a nation that did righteousness," thus answers to, "they ask of Me just judgments" (that is, as a matter of justice due to them, salvation to themselves, and destruction to their enemies); and "forsook not the ordinance of their God," answers to "they desire the drawing near of God" (that God would draw near to exercise those "just judgments" in behalf of them, and against their enemies) [Maurer]. So Jerome, "In the confidence, as it were, of a good conscience, they demand a just judgment, in the language of the saints: Judge me, O Lord, for I have walked in mine integrity." So in Mal 2:17, they affect to be scandalized at the impunity of the wicked, and impugn God's justice [Horsley]. Thus, "seek Me daily, and desire (English Version not so well, 'delight') to know My ways," refers to their requiring to know why God delayed so long in helping them. English Version gives a good, though different sense; namely, dispelling the delusion that God would be satisfied with outward observances, while the spirit of the law, was violated and the heart unchanged (<reference osisRef="Isa.58.3-Isa.58.14">Is 58:3-14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.33.31">Eze 33:31</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezek.33.32">32</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="John.18.28">Joh 18:28</reference>), scrupulosity side by side with murder. The prophets were the commentators on the law, as their Magna Charta, in its inward spirit and not the mere letter. <div eID="gen16311" type="x-p"/>
entries.3bf25f210a5132bed9f6621e416e47457af5adea: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9415"/><div sID="gen16312" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9415"/><hi type="bold">3. Wherefore--</hi>the words of the Jews: "Why is it that, when we fast, Thou dost not notice it" (by delivering us)? They think to lay God under obligation to their fasting (<reference osisRef="Ps.73.13">Psa 73:13</reference>; Mal 3:14).<div eID="gen16312" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16313" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">afflicted ... soul--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Lev.16.29">Le 16:29</reference>).<div eID="gen16313" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16314" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Behold--</hi>God's reply.<div eID="gen16314" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16315" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">pleasure--</hi>in antithesis to their boast of having "afflicted their soul"; it was only in outward show they really enjoyed themselves. Gesenius not so well translates, "business."<div eID="gen16315" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16316" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">exact ... labours--</hi>rather, "oppressive labors" [Maurer]. Horsley, with Vulgate, translates, "Exact the whole upon your debtors"; those who owe you labor (<reference osisRef="Neh.5.1-Neh.5.8">Ne 5:1-5, 8</reference>-10, &c.). <div eID="gen16316" type="x-p"/>
entries.4dd5e846dbb1c6d72513a7f566426e05e4e538db: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9416"/><div sID="gen16317" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9416"/><hi type="bold">4. ye shall not fast--</hi>rather, "ye do not fast at this time, so as to make your voice to be heard on high," that is, in heaven; your aim in fasting is strife, not to gain the ear of God [Maurer] (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.21.9">1Ki 21:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.12.13">12, 13</reference>). In English Version the sense is, If you wish acceptance with God, ye must not fast as ye now do, to make your voice heard high in strife. <div eID="gen16317" type="x-p"/>
entries.49bd1e481dfd21cd759b9ec560fc117a6897b27d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9417"/><div sID="gen16318" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9417"/><hi type="bold">5. for a man to afflict his soul--</hi>The pain felt by abstinence is not the end to be sought, as if it were meritorious; it is of value only in so far as it leads us to amend our ways (<reference osisRef="Isa.58.6">Is 58:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.58.7">7</reference>).<div eID="gen16318" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16319" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">bow ... head ... sackcloth--</hi>to affect the outward tokens, so as to "appear to men to fast" (<reference osisRef="Matt.6.17">Mt 6:17</reference>, <reference osisRef="Matt.6.18">18</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Kgs.21.27">1Ki 21:27</reference>; <reference osisRef="Esth.4.3">Es 4:3</reference>). <div eID="gen16319" type="x-p"/>
entries.6218706f6469866dee1b91a176f879b877e88905: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9418"/><div sID="gen16320" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9418"/><hi type="bold">6. loose ... bands of wickedness--</hi>that is, to dissolve every tie wherewith one has unjustly bound his fellow men (<reference osisRef="Lev.25.49">Le 25:49</reference>, &c.). Servitude, a fraudulent contract, &c.<div eID="gen16320" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16321" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">undo ... heavy burdens--</hi>Hebrew, "loose the bands of the yoke."<div eID="gen16321" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16322" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">oppressed--</hi>literally, "the broken." The expression, "to let go free," implies that those "broken" with the yoke of slavery, are meant (<reference osisRef="Neh.5.10-Neh.5.12">Ne 5:10-12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.34.9-Jer.11.14">Jr 34:9-11, 14</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.11.16">16</reference>). Jerome interprets it, broken with poverty; bankrupt. <div eID="gen16322" type="x-p"/>
entries.8a82cef4e854f5b1201fb9977fe10dd55bb7eb8c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9419"/><div sID="gen16323" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9419"/><hi type="bold">7. deal--</hi>distribute (<reference osisRef="Job.31.16-Job.31.21">Job 31:16-21</reference>).<div eID="gen16323" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16324" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">cast out--</hi>rather, reduced [Horsley].<div eID="gen16324" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16325" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">naked ... cover him--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Matt.25.36">Mt 25:36</reference>).<div eID="gen16325" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16326" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">hide ... thyself--</hi>means to be strange towards them, and not to relieve them in their poverty (<reference osisRef="Matt.15.5">Mt 15:5</reference>).<div eID="gen16326" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16327" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">flesh--</hi>kindred (<reference osisRef="Gen.29.14">Ge 29:14</reference>). Also brethren in common descent from Adam, and brethren in Christ (<reference osisRef="Jas.2.15">Jas 2:15</reference>). <div eID="gen16327" type="x-p"/>
entries.7a3090fd1b4c4e827030d1d0c117815dcf82ec68: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9420"/><div sID="gen16328" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9420"/><hi type="bold">8. light--</hi>emblem of prosperity (<reference osisRef="Isa.58.10">Is 58:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.11.17">Job 11:17</reference>).<div eID="gen16328" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16329" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">health--</hi>literally, a long bandage, applied by surgeons to heal a wound (compare <reference osisRef="Isa.1.6">Is 1:6</reference>). Hence restoration from all past calamities.<div eID="gen16329" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16330" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">go before thee--</hi>Thy conformity to the divine covenant acts as a leader, conducting thee to peace and prosperity.<div eID="gen16330" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16331" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">glory ... reward--</hi>like the pillar of cloud and fire, the symbol of God's "glory," which went behind Israel, separating them from their Egyptian pursuers (<reference osisRef="Isa.52.12">Is 52:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Exod.14.19">Ex 14:19</reference>, <reference osisRef="Exod.14.20">20</reference>). <div eID="gen16331" type="x-p"/>
entries.dce7ed3976325e13691a4bc1479483d648cecd08: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9421"/><div sID="gen16332" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9421"/><hi type="bold">9. Then ... call ... answer--</hi>when sin is renounced (<reference osisRef="Isa.65.24">Is 65:24</reference>). When the Lord's call is not hearkened to, He will not hear our "call" (<reference osisRef="Ps.66.18">Psa 66:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.1.24">Pr 1:24</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.28">28</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.15.29">15:29</reference>; 28:9).<div eID="gen16332" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16333" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">putting forth of ... finger--</hi>the finger of scorn pointed at simple-minded godly men. The middle finger was so used by the Romans.<div eID="gen16333" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16334" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">speaking vanity--</hi>every injurious speech [Lowth]. <div eID="gen16334" type="x-p"/>
entries.b4cac809bbba8dbe15e76d1a5955687bf3c94b35: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9422"/><div sID="gen16335" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9422"/><hi type="bold">10. draw out thy soul--</hi>"impart of thine own subsistence," or "sustenance" [Horsley]. "Soul" is figurative for "that wherewith thou sustainest thy soul," or "life."<div eID="gen16335" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16336" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">light ... in obscurity--</hi>Calamities shall be suddenly succeeded by prosperity (<reference osisRef="Ps.112.4">Psa 112:4</reference>). <div eID="gen16336" type="x-p"/>
entries.1ed965bd509ee020398843877abe290ad1409d1a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9423"/><div sID="gen16337" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9423"/><hi type="bold">11. satisfy ... in drought--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Isa.41.17">Is 41:17</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.41.18">18</reference>). Literally, "drought," that is, parched places [Maurer].<div eID="gen16337" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16338" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">make fat--</hi>rather, "strengthen" [Noyes]. "Give thee the free use of thy bones" [Jerome], or, "of thy strength" [Horsley].<div eID="gen16338" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16339" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">watered garden--</hi>an Oriental picture of happiness.<div eID="gen16339" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16340" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">fail not--</hi>Hebrew, "deceive not"; as streams that disappoint the caravan which had expected to find water, as formerly, but find it dried up (<reference osisRef="Job.6.15-Job.6.17">Job 6:15-17</reference>). <div eID="gen16340" type="x-p"/>
entries.6307102b60b45df473fdb90439631fb15fd56cae: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9424"/><div sID="gen16341" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9424"/><hi type="bold">12. they ... of thee--</hi>thy people, the Israelites.<div eID="gen16341" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16342" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">old waste places--</hi>the old ruins of Jerusalem (<reference osisRef="Isa.61.4">Is 61:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.36.33-Ezek.36.36">Eze 36:33-36</reference>).<div eID="gen16342" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16343" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">foundations of many generations--</hi>that is, the buildings which had lain in ruins, even to their foundations, for many ages; called in the parallel passage (<reference osisRef="Isa.61.4">Is 61:4</reference>), "the former desolations"; and in the preceding clause here, "the old waste places." The literal and spiritual restoration of Israel is meant, which shall produce like blessed results on the Gentile world (<reference osisRef="Amos.9.11">Am 9:11</reference>, <reference osisRef="Amos.9.12">12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.15.16">Ac 15:16</reference>, <reference osisRef="Acts.15.17">17</reference>).<div eID="gen16343" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16344" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">be called--</hi>appropriately: the name truly designating what thou shalt do.<div eID="gen16344" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16345" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">breach--</hi>the calamity wherewith God visited Israel for their sin (<reference osisRef="Isa.30.26">Is 30:26</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Chr.15.13">1Ch 15:13</reference>).<div eID="gen16345" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16346" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">paths to dwell in--</hi>not that the paths were to be dwelt in, but the paths leading to their dwellings were to be restored; "paths, so as to dwell in the land" [Maurer]. <div eID="gen16346" type="x-p"/>
entries.6bf59ff7ef04f1f424bf296c45c1870f0a4e3b0f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9425"/><div sID="gen16347" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9425"/>13. (<reference osisRef="Isa.56.2">Is 56:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Neh.13.15-Neh.13.22">Ne 13:15-22</reference>). The Sabbath, even under the new dispensation, was to be obligatory (<reference osisRef="Isa.66.23">Is 66:23</reference>).<div eID="gen16347" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16348" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">foot--</hi>the instrument of motion (compare <reference osisRef="Prov.4.27">Pr 4:27</reference>); men are not to travel for mere pleasure on the Sabbath (<reference osisRef="Acts.1.12">Ac 1:12</reference>). The Jews were forbidden to travel on it farther than the tabernacle or temple. If thou keep thy foot from going on thy own ways and "doing thy pleasure," &c. (<reference osisRef="Exod.20.10">Ex 20:10</reference>, <reference osisRef="Exod.20.11">11</reference>).<div eID="gen16348" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16349" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">my holy day--</hi>God claims it as His day; to take it for our pleasure is to rob Him of His own. This is the very way in which the Sabbath is mostly broken; it is made a day of carnal pleasure instead of spiritual "delight."<div eID="gen16349" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16350" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">holy of the Lord--</hi>not the predicate, but the subject; "if thou call the holy (day) of Jehovah honorable"; if thou treat it as a day to be honored.<div eID="gen16350" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16351" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">him--</hi>or else, it, the Sabbath.<div eID="gen16351" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16352" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">not doing ... own way--</hi>answering to, "turn away thy foot from the Sabbath."<div eID="gen16352" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16353" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">nor finding ... pleasure--</hi>answering to, "doing thy pleasure." "To keep the Sabbath in an idle manner is the sabbath of oxen and asses; to pass it in a jovial manner is the sabbath of the golden calf, when the people sat down to eat and drink, and rose again to play; to keep it in surfeiting and wantonness is the sabbath of Satan, the devil's holiday" [Bishop Andrewes].<div eID="gen16353" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16354" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">nor speaking ... words--</hi>answering to, "call Sabbath a delight ... honorable." Man's "own words" would "call" it a "weariness"; it is the spiritual nature given from above which "calls it a delight" (<reference osisRef="Amos.8.5">Am 8:5</reference>; Mal 1:13). <div eID="gen16354" type="x-p"/>
entries.d16a196cc84f9d93d29ec44b8b8bb163f2e11c71: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9426"/><div sID="gen16355" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9426"/><hi type="bold">14. delight ... in ... Lord--</hi>God rewards in kind, as He punishes in kind. As we "delight" in keeping God's "Sabbath," so God will give us "delight" in Himself (<reference osisRef="Gen.15.1">Ge 15:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.22.21-Job.22.26">Job 22:21-26</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.37.4">Psa 37:4</reference>).<div eID="gen16355" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16356" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">ride upon ... high places--</hi>I will make thee supreme lord of the land; the phrase is taken from a conqueror riding in his chariot, and occupying the hills and fastnesses of a country [Vitringa], (<reference osisRef="Deut.32.13">De 32:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Mic.1.3">Mi 1:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Hab.3.19">Ha 3:19</reference>). Judea was a land of hills; the idea thus is, "I will restore thee to thine own land" [Calvin]. The parallel words, "heritage of Jacob," confirm this (<reference osisRef="Gen.27.28">Ge 27:28</reference>, <reference osisRef="Gen.27.29">29</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gen.28.13-Gen.28.15">28:13-15</reference>).<div eID="gen16356" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16357" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">mouth of ... Lord ... spoken it--</hi>a formula to assure men of the fulfilment of any solemn promise which God has made (<reference osisRef="Isa.40.5">Is 40:5</reference>). <chapter eID="Isa.58"/>

entries.1ae2ad0a3b7ddf3c8880d3082b63ed6c5833c05c: <div eID="gen28807" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen28808" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen28809" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen28809" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen28808" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen28810" type="x-p"/> This elegant chapter contains a severe reproof of the Jews on account of their vices, particularly their hypocrisy in practising and relying on outward ceremonies, such as fasting and bodily humiliation, without true repentance, <reference osisRef="Isa.58.1-Isa.58.5">Isa 58:1-5</reference>. It then lays down a clear and comprehensive summary of the duties they owed to their fellow creatures, <reference osisRef="Isa.58.6">Isa 58:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.58.7">Isa 58:7</reference>. Large promises of happiness and prosperity are likewise annexed to the performance of these duties in a variety of the most beautiful and striking images, <reference osisRef="Isa.58.8-Isa.58.12">Isa 58:8-12</reference>. Great temporal and spiritual blessedness of those who keep holy the Sabbath day, <reference osisRef="Isa.58.13">Isa 58:13</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.58.14">Isa 58:14</reference>. <div eID="gen28810" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28811" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen28811" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28812" type="x-p"/> Cry aloud, spare not - Never was a louder cry against the hypocrisy, nor a more cutting reproof of the wickedness, of a people professing a national established religion, having all the forms of godliness without a particle of its power. This chapter has been often appointed to be read on political fast days for the success of wars carried on for - God knows what purposes, and originating in - God knows what motives. Politically speaking, was ever any thing more injudicious?
entries.bd9825fe0f5c74d2ad4f8544fda8cb4bfddc38d7: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen28812" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28813" type="x-p"/> Have we adopted our soul "Have we afflicted our souls" - Twenty-seven MSS. (six ancient) of Dr. Kennicott's, thirty-six of De Rossi's, and two of my own, and the old edition of 1488 have the noun in the plural number, נפשינו naphsheynu, our souls; and so the Septuagint, Chaldee, and Vulgate. This reading is undoubtedly genuine. <div eID="gen28813" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28814" type="x-p"/> In the day of your fast ye find pleasure - Fast days are generally called holidays, and holidays are days of idleness and pleasure. In numberless cases the fast is turned into a feast. <div eID="gen28814" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28815" type="x-p"/> And exact all your labors - Some disregard the most sacred fast, and will oblige their servant to work all day long; others use fast days for the purpose of settling their accounts, posting up their books, and drawing out their bills to be ready to collect their debts. These are sneaking hypocrites; the others are daringly irreligious.
entries.e802a41de2ba8bb042daa10d797eb6c33b33d52a: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen28815" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28816" type="x-p"/> Ye fast for strife and debate - How often is this the case! A whole nation are called to fast to implore God's blessing on wars carried on for the purposes of wrath and ambition. <div eID="gen28816" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28817" type="x-p"/> To smite with the fist of wickedness: ye shall not fast as ye do this day "To smite with the fist the poor. Wherefore fast ye unto me in this manner" - I follow the version of the Septuagint, which gives a much better sense than the present reading of the Hebrew. Instead of רשע לא resha lo, they seem to have read in their copy רש על מה לי rash al mah lli. The four first letters are the same, but otherwise divided in regard to the words; the four last are lost, and א aleph added in their place, in order to make some sort of sense with רשע ל. The version of the Septuagint is, και τυπτετε τυγμαις ταπεινον· ἱνα τι μοι νηστευετε - as above.
entries.529cb892c51ec3021348b695cca3a5162a7e9782: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen28817" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28818" type="x-p"/> Let the oppressed go free - How can any nation pretend to fast or worship God at all, or dare to profess that they believe in the existence of such a Being, while they carry on the slave trade, and traffic in the souls, blood, and bodies, of men! O ye most flagitious of knaves, and worst of hypocrites, cast off at once the mask of religion; and deepen not your endless perdition by professing the faith of our Lord Jesus Christ, while ye continue in this traffic!
entries.5fa10e34fe5417c7dd2fee3ae5de7f720fd21ad4: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen28818" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28819" type="x-p"/> Deal thy bread to the hungry - But this thou canst not do, if thou eat it thyself. When a man fasts, suppose he do it through a religious motive, he should give the food of that day, from which he abstains, to the poor and hungry, who, in the course of providence, are called to sustain many involuntary fasts, besides suffering general privations. Wo to him who saves a day's victuals by his religious fast! He should either give them or their value in money to the poor. See <reference osisRef="Isa.58.6">Isa 58:6</reference>. <div eID="gen28819" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28820" type="x-p"/> That thou bring the poor that are cast out to thy house "To bring the wandering poor into thy house" - πτωχους αστεγους, Septuagint; egenos vagosque, Vulgate; and מטלטלין metaltelin, Chaldee. They read, instead of מרודים merudim, הנודים hanudim. מר mer is upon a rasure in the Bodleian MS. The same MS. reads ביתה bayethah, in domum, "into the house." - L.
entries.00687899eb8111d09deb7630cf5316b4c3581295: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen28820" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28821" type="x-p"/> And thine health shall spring forth speedily "And thy wounds shall speedily be healed over" - Et cicatrix vulneris tui cito obducetur "And the scar of thy wounds shall be speedily removed." Aquila's Version, as reported by Jerome, with which agrees that of the Chaldee. <div eID="gen28821" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28822" type="x-p"/> The glory "And the glory" - Sixteen MSS. (five ancient) of Dr. Kennicott's, and the Septuagint, Syriac, and Vulgate add the conjunction ו vau, וכבוד vechabod.
entries.5ecdfc71244f24661deaad43e9d6876a4e1c78cb: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen28822" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28823" type="x-p"/> And if thou draw out thy soul to the hungry "If thou bring forth thy bread to the hungry" - "To draw out thy soul to the hungry," as our translators rightly enough express the present Hebrew text, is an obscure phrase, and without example in any other place. But instead of נפשך naphshecha, thy soul, eight MSS. (three ancient) of Kennicott's and three of De Rossi's read לחמך lachmecha, thy bread; and so the Syriac renders it. The Septuagint express both words, τον αρτον εκ της ψυχης σου, "thy bread from thy soul." I cannot help thinking, however, that this reading is a gloss, and should not be adopted. To draw out the soul in relieving the poor, is to do it, not of constraint or necessity, but cheerfully, and is both nervous and elegant. His soul pities and his hand gives.
entries.8a23b95aadc246a2c65ce9e5ecfd4831d2a2db04: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen28823" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28824" type="x-p"/> And make fat thy bones "And he shall renew thy strength" - Chaldaeus forte legit יחכיף עצמתך yachaliph otsmathecha; confer cap. <reference osisRef="Isa.40.29">Isa 40:29</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.40.31">Isa 40:31</reference>, et <reference osisRef="Isa.41.1">Isa 41:1</reference>. - Secker. "The Chaldee perhaps read יחליף עצמתך yachaliph otsmathecha. "The Chaldee has וגופך יחיי בחיי עלמא veguphach vechaiyey bechaiyey alma, "and he will vivify thy body in life eternal." The rest of the ancients seem not to know what to make of יחליץ yachalits; and the rendering of the Vulgate, which seems to be the only proper one, ossa tua liberabit, "he will deliver thy bones," makes no sense. I follow this excellent emendation; to favor which it is still farther to be observed that three MSS., instead of עצמתיך atsmotheycha, have עצמתך otsmathecha, singular. - L.
entries.6fa47569ee95459a2d1e6a73410ddceeee42e4c2: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen28824" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28825" type="x-p"/> The restorer of paths to dwell in "The restorer of paths to be frequented by inhabitants" - To this purpose it is rendered by the Syriac, Symmachus, and Theodotion.
entries.0712680d24c58e5f24f5a906ef1a56e1eb48c9a0: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen28825" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28826" type="x-p"/> If thou turn away thy foot from the Sabbath - The meaning of this seems to be, that they should be careful not to take their pleasure on the Sabbath day, by paying visits, and taking country jaunts; not going, as Kimchi interprets it, more than a Sabbath day's journey, which was only two thousand cubits beyond the city's suburbs. How vilely is this rule transgressed by the inhabitants of this land! They seem to think that the Sabbath was made only for their recreation! <div eID="gen28826" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28827" type="x-p"/> From doing thy pleasure - The Septuagint, Syriac, and Chaldee, for עשות asoth, manifestly express מעשות measoth. So likewise a MS. has it, but with the omission of the words שבת רגלך shabbath raglecha. - L. <div eID="gen28827" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28828" type="x-p"/> The holy of the Lord "And the holy feast of Jehovah" - Twenty-eight MSS.
